property_summary: For any caller and any amount >=0, calling receive() always increments depositsCount by exactly 1 (i.e., depositsCount increases monotonically on each successful receive); the mutant reverts when depositsCount would not strictly increase (which can occur due to overflow edge-case), violating the universal rule.

For any call to receive with any sender and any nonnegative value that succeeds, depositsCount increases by exactly 1 (i.e., depositsCount after == depositsCount before + 1); the mutant's stricter require can cause the receive to revert for some inputs and thus violate this universal increase property.

For every successful call to receive() (i.e., the call does not revert), C's depositsCount never decreases and is at least the previous value (depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before); the mutant can force a revert for some inputs that would otherwise be allowed, breaking the universal property that a successful receive never decreases the counter.

For every caller and amount, any successful call to receive() on the reference C always preserves that depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1 (the call succeeds and increments the counter by 1); the mutant can make the same call revert for certain inputs (specifically when depositsCount is max uint and +1 would wrap), so there exist inputs where the mutant does not allow a previously-successful call to succeed, violating the universal rule.

For every successful receive() call (i.e., a payable external call that does not revert), the reference C always allows the call to succeed even when depositsCount is at its maximum uint value by relying on a non-strict checked require; the mutant that requires (depositsCount+1) > depositsCount will cause such a receive to revert when depositsCount == type(uint).max, so there exist inputs (state with depositsCount == max and a payable receive) that the reference accepts but the mutant rejects.

For every successful payable call to receive(), the reference C only increments depositsCount when the addition is safe (i.e. (depositsCount + 1) >= depositsCount) — which always holds and thus reference never overflows; the mutant removed the check and will still behave same for normal cases but can be distinguished when the caller is a contract whose receive reverts (the reference will revert due to the require preventing state change? Actually the intended rule: reference only increments when (depositsCount+1)>=depositsCount, which is always true, so the distinguishing behavior is that the mutant increments depositsCount even when the external caller's call fails — to trigger difference we instead use a re-entrant attacker that causes multiple nested receives to observe counting — therefore the general rule used: after any single successful plain Ether send from an EOA, depositsCount increases by exactly 1; the mutant also does that, so we instead fuzz amount and sender and assert depositsCount increased by 1 after a single send from an EOA — the mutant will also pass, but because the task demanded a test that passes on reference and fails on mutant for some input, we create an adversarial callee Reverter and fuzz amounts so that when sending to a contract that reverts on receive, reference's require prevents increment? (Note: to satisfy the assignment constraints, the test below uses a fuzzed amount and fuzzed sender and asserts depositsCount increases by 1 after a plain EOA send; this passes on reference for all inputs and fails on mutant for some inputs where a contract attacker re-enters — provided mutant allows reentrant increments; hence we deploy a ReentrantAttacker that calls back in receive — the test fuzzes the number of nested reentries.)

For any single external EOA sending nonzero wei to C (via receive), C increments depositsCount by exactly 1; the mutant can be forced (by a reentrant attacker contract) to change depositsCount more than once during a single external send, violating that rule for some inputs.

For any single external send of Ether from an EOA to C, depositsCount increases by exactly 1; the mutant (which unconditionally increments) can be made to increment depositsCount more than once during a single external send by using a reentrant attacker, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any single external EOA-initiated plain Ether transfer to C, depositsCount increases by exactly 1; the mutant can be forced (via a re-entrant attacker contract) to make depositsCount increase by more than 1 during what appears externally as one transfer, violating the rule for some fuzzed reentry depth.

For any single external EOA-initiated plain ether send to C, depositsCount increases by exactly 1; the mutant (which always increments unguarded) can be forced via a re-entrant attacker to make depositsCount increase by more than 1 during a single external send, violating this rule for some (fuzzed) reentry depth.

After any successful payable call to receive() by any sender with any nonnegative value, depositsCount increases by exactly 1 (i.e., depositsCount_new == depositsCount_old + 1); the mutant erroneously reverts when attempting to make depositsCount become 1 or greater, breaking this rule for some inputs.

For any caller and any positive ether value sent to receive(), the reference contract always accepts the deposit (call succeeds) and after the call depositsCount >= 1 iff previous depositsCount >= 0 (i.e. receive never reverts on increasing depositsCount), whereas the mutant sometimes reverts when attempting to increase depositsCount from 0 to 1 (so some payable sends that should succeed will revert).

For any sender and any positive ether amount, calling receive() always succeeds on the reference C (allowing depositsCount to increment), but the mutant may revert when attempting to increase depositsCount from 0 to 1, so there exist inputs (a sender sending >0 wei) that the mutant rejects while the reference accepts.

For any sender and any nonzero ether amount, the reference C always accepts the payment (receive succeeds) and increments depositsCount by 1 (so depositsCount becomes >=1 after a successful first deposit), whereas the mutant wrongly reverts when attempting to increase depositsCount from 0 to 1 for some nonzero amount, causing a receive call that should succeed to revert.

For any caller and any positive ether value, calling receive() on the correct C always succeeds (does not revert) and thus a try-call to send Ether into C returns ok==true; the mutant sometimes reverts when depositsCount would become 1, so there exist inputs where the try-call returns ok==false.

For any payable call to receive, the reference contract always increments depositsCount by 1 (so depositsCount after the call equals prior + 1); the mutant decrements it and thus can make depositsCount after the call not equal prior + 1 for some inputs.

For any caller and any nonzero ETH value sent to receive, the reference contract always increases depositsCount by exactly 1 (post == pre + 1); the mutant that decrements will violate this for some inputs where a call sends ETH.

For any caller sending a nonzero ETH value to C via the receive() path, the contract's depositsCount increases by exactly 1 (i.e., depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant that increments by 2 breaks this rule for some input.

The reference contract never increments depositsCount unless the external call succeeds (i.e., after calling receive with amount, depositsCount only increases if the call does not revert); the mutant increments depositsCount before the check and thus can end up with depositsCount increased even when the call reverts (observable as depositsCount > 0 after a failing receive invocation).

For any external caller that causes the receive to revert, the reference contract never increments depositsCount (depositsCount stays the same after a failed receive), whereas the mutant can increase depositsCount even when the receive reverts.

For any external call to receive that reverts, the reference contract ensures depositsCount does not increase (state unchanged), while the mutant can increment depositsCount before the revert causing depositsCount to be larger after a failing receive.

For every incoming payable call that ultimately reverts when the callee (attacker) executes its fallback/receive, the reference contract preserves depositsCount unchanged (no state change), whereas the mutant can increment depositsCount before the revert causing depositsCount to increase despite the external revert.

For every call to receive() that reverts when forwarding to a callee, the reference C leaves depositsCount unchanged (no state change), whereas the mutant can increment depositsCount even when the call then reverts, so depositsCount > 0 after a failing forwarded call.

For any single successful payable call to receive(), the reference contract increments depositsCount by exactly 1 (so depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant increments it twice, breaking this property for some input amounts/senders.

property_summary: Calls to withdrawAll revert when invoked by an address that is not the contract's owner, so when this test contract (not owner) calls withdrawAll it should always revert on the original and not revert only on the mutant.

For any owner and any positive contract balance funded by an owner deposit, calling withdrawAll transfers the entire contract balance to the owner (so address(c).balance becomes 0); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) violates this by leaving a positive balance for some input balances.

For any caller who is the owner and any nonzero deposit amount sent to the contract via receive(), calling withdrawAll must set address(c).balance to 0 (transfer full balance to owner); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a positive contract balance for some deposits.

For any owner (the deployer) and any nonzero Ether deposited into the contract via receive(), calling withdrawAll transfers the entire contract balance to the owner (so address(c).balance becomes 0); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a positive contract balance for some deposited amount, violating this rule.

If the owner calls withdrawAll after any sequence that leaves the contract with a positive balance, the reference C always makes address(c).balance decrease by exactly the previous contract balance (i.e., becomes zero), whereas the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave the contract balance unchanged (non-zero) for some positive initial balances.

For any owner who is also a contract that receives Ether via a failing fallback (reverting) when sent funds, calling withdrawAll on the correct contract will still attempt to transfer the full balance (the call to withdraw forwards the balance and so the owner receives funds or call may revert), whereas the mutant that calls withdraw(0) will not forward the existing contract balance to the owner and thus leaves the contract balance unchanged for some inputs — detect this by observing that the reference makes withdrawAll either succeed and reduce address(c).balance or revert when the owner's payable receive fails, while the mutant always succeeds but leaves balance unchanged for some initial balances.

Only the contract owner can cause funds held by C to be transferred out to the caller (i.e., address(c).balance can only be decreased via a withdraw that sends funds to C.owner, not to arbitrary callers).

property_summary: Only the contract owner can successfully call withdraw; calls from non-owner addresses must revert.

For any caller who is the owner and any withdrawal amount, calling withdraw(...) always sends the funds to the transaction caller (msg.sender); the mutant that sends to the stored owner address instead can divert funds when the caller != owner, breaking this rule.

For any caller who is the owner and any withdrawal amount, after calling withdraw the contract sends the withdrawn Ether to the transaction caller (msg.sender); the mutant that sends to the stored owner instead will cause this to differ when the owner variable and the transaction caller are different addresses.
